15.0.0.en: After the trial of the Lord before the Jewish assembly in the house of Caiaphas the high priest, and the council of the seventy (the Sanhedrin – see Mt 5:21-22), the highest Jewish authority, the decision was made to be rid of Him. Since the death sentence was the prerogative of the Roman governor and not of the Jews, they held the Lord Jesus bound until morning, so that they might take Him to the Roman governor's residence and present Him to Pilate the governor.

15.1.0.en: Pilate's question here, "Art thou the King of the Jews?", may have come from what he had heard earlier about the procession in which the crowds received the Lord on the previous Sunday when He entered Jerusalem, or from the accusation of the chief priests that the charge against this man was rebellion against Roman rule and a desire to set himself up as king. As for Christ's answer, "Thou sayest it," it is a Jewish expression meaning agreement, and what is meant, of course, is a spiritual kingship, since Christ had already declared that He is from above and that His kingdom is not of this world (Jn 8:23, 18:36).

15.2.0.en: St. Mark was more concise in his Gospel than the other Evangelists, so he said nothing about Pilate's wife, or the washing of his hands, or the details of the accusations against the Lord Jesus, but was content to say that they were many. In the face of these many accusations, Pilate offered the Lord a chance to defend Himself, but Christ preferred silence to speech, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled: "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter" (53:7). As for Pilate, he marvelled greatly at the Lord's refusal to speak.

15.3.0.en: Pilate was accustomed to release to the Jews at every feast one of those who had been arrested, because it was the duty of the Roman authority to settle Jewish disturbances. At that time the one called Barabbas was bound (imprisoned), for he was a murderer in one of the riots, and he was condemned to crucifixion and awaiting death.

15.4.0.en: St. Matthew explains in his Gospel (27:17) that Pilate gave the people the choice of releasing one of the two (the Lord Jesus or Barabbas). He set this choice in the hope that the crowd would ask for the release of the Lord Jesus, but these people were Jews loyal to the priests and the rulers, and they feared them.

15.5.0.en: This verse explains the reason for what Pilate did in giving the people a choice between (the Lord and Barabbas), for he knew the motive of the wicked chief priests, and that he had found in Christ no cause that deserved death.

15.6.0.en: The feelings of rage, envy and evil burning inside the hearts of the priests drove them to influence the crowds of people who were led along behind them, so that all demanded the release of Barabbas. And when Pilate asked the crowd what should become of Christ, they all cried out: "Crucify him," which was the Roman punishment for the rebellious slave.

15.7.0.en: Pilate found nothing in all that he had heard sufficient for the crucifixion of Christ, and he expressed this by asking them: "Why, what evil hath he done?" Yet this question did nothing but increase their agitation against Him and their insistence all the more on the crucifixion of Christ.

15.8.0.en: Here too, briefly, St. Mark passes over the events quickly, yet he did not fail to mention that Pilate sentenced Christ without conviction, but "to content" them, violating his conscience thereby and fearing the riot that might occur (Mt 27:24); and if this riot turned into a revolt, it might topple him from his seat. For this reason he ordered the Lord Jesus to be scourged and handed over to be crucified.

15.8.1.en: My dear friend ... notice with me how many times opportunities were given to acquit the Lord and release Him. First Pilate gave them a choice between Him and Barabbas, but they chose to acquit the wicked rather than the good. Then another time he declared plainly before them: "Why, what evil hath he done?" in an attempt to awaken their consciences, and yet they did not draw back from their evil, but grew more insistent.

15.8.2.en: My brother ... we are not here to judge the Jews, but to take a lesson and instruction. The first is: not to make a decision while we are in a state of agitation and anger. The second is: not to ignore God's calls to correct our decisions. And the last is: not to be led by anyone's influence over our consciences, but to examine them well before God alone. And remember that: "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the Lord" (Prov 17:15).

15.8.3.en: If I ask myself, who is responsible for the crucifixion of Christ?! In this scene we find that Judas betrayed Him, the religious leaders demanded His death, Peter denied Him, the disciples left Him in fear, Pilate feared for his seat, the crowds were passive and did nothing, and the soldiers mocked Him, struck Him and tortured Him! So what about me if I were exposed to the same situation?! What a hard and difficult question!!!

15.9.0.en: "The whole band": the Roman cohort was made up of six hundred soldiers, who all gathered around Christ in the courtyard of the Roman governor's residence and made Christ an amusement for themselves, mocking Him. "Purple": the purple robe, or scarlet as Matthew called it, is a red-coloured robe that kings used to wear.

15.9.1.en: "A crown of thorns": they made from a stem (or branch) of a thorny plant known as "al-balan" a round crown (a cap) and put it on His head. St. Matthew adds (27:29) that they put "a reed in his right hand," to complete their mockery of Him, since they made Him look like the kings. And in their ridicule, they saluted Him and offered Him a greeting as the King of the Jews.

15.9.2.en: Among the beautiful symbolic reflections is that His garments which they took off point to the casting off and rejection of the Jewish nation, while the red robe signifies the blood of Christ, by which He redeems us and by which He reigns over our hearts.

15.9.3.en: Notice also the Jewish nation's persistence in rejection, for it had already cut off its ears from listening to the Lord (see the commentary on 14:46-47).

15.10.0.en: Continuing this sad scene, shameful for all humanity, which mocks its Creator, its Governor and its Redeemer, the soldiers of the band dared to attack the Lord by striking His head in the worst form of insult, and they spat on Him, and bowed down in mockery of the title of King. And after this very painful scene, they took off Him the purple robe and put His own garments on Him, and then led Him out to the way of the Cross.

15.10.1.en: O my soul ... what can you say before this wonderful scene, beyond description ... who is mocking whom, and why all this, is it not because of you ... is it not for your liberation?! And in return, what are you doing ... do you keep the favour ... or do you still pain Him with your many sins?!

15.10.2.en: Repent, O my soul, and do not forget the sufferings of your Saviour, for if they remain before you, I do not think you will dare to do wrong ... Forgive us, O holy Saviour ... and we thank You for all that You endured for our sake.

15.11.0.en: Christ carried His cross at the beginning of the way (Jn 19:17), and when exhaustion overtook Him, because of the scourging, the staying awake all night and the many trials, the Roman soldiers compelled a Jewish man who had grown up in Cyrene – in northern Libya – so that his title became the Cyrenian. It seems that his sons Alexander and Rufus became known to the community of Christians afterward, since St. Mark took care to mention their names.

15.12.0.en: "Golgotha": that is, "skull," a place outside Jerusalem. Some say that it is a high rock formation resembling a human skull, and others say that the reason for its being so named is the Jews' belief that the skull of Adam was buried in this place.

15.13.0.en: "Wine mingled with myrrh": myrrh was one of the strong and well-known painkillers that reaches a degree of anaesthesia, and it was mixed with wine – which resembles vinegar in taste because of its cheap price (see the commentary on Mt 27:34) – so that it would be easy to take, and it was usually offered to the crucified to relieve some of his pain, but Christ refused it so that His sufferings might be completed!!

15.14.0.en: "They crucified him": they lifted up Christ, nailing His hands and feet, upon the wood of the Cross. And the suffering of pain began, and the flow of blood inside and outside His body, as a result of the difficulty of breathing while nailed. It was the right of the Roman soldiers to take the garments of the one they crucified, so they took off His garments – and He became naked who covers all creation with His mercies – and the Roman soldiers divided His garments among themselves by casting lots for them ... in a clear reference to what David prophesied in his psalm (22:18): "and upon my vesture they cast lots."

15.15.0.en: St. John says, and tradition holds, that the crucifixion was about the sixth hour (which begins at twelve noon – Jn 19:14), whereas Mark, by saying here the third hour (which begins at nine in the morning), means the procedures for the beginning of the crucifixion, which took some time, and it is most likely that the Cross was fully raised shortly before the sixth hour, near the end of the third hour.

15.15.1.en: It is noted that in Jewish timekeeping there are no breaks between the third hour and the sixth hour, so the end of the first is the beginning of the second, like the difference between morning and noon in our present timekeeping.

15.16.0.en: "His accusation": it was customary for the crucified to carry with his cross his accusation (that is, the cause of his crime and crucifixion). And since Pilate found no cause worthy of crucifixion, he made the accusation that was hung on the cross with the crucified one: "This is Jesus the King of the Jews," and he wrote it in the three languages spread in the region at that time, which are Hebrew, Greek and Latin. And some add that Pilate wrote this to provoke the Jews, that their king had been crucified.

15.17.0.en: The death sentence was also carried out by crucifixion on two thieves who deserved the sentence, so they put one on His right and the other on His left, thereby fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah that: "He was numbered with the transgressors" (53:12), and perhaps in the crucifixion of the two thieves there is an indication that the redemption of Christ includes all the Jews and the Gentiles.

15.18.0.en: In mockery and ridicule, all who passed by blasphemed at the sight of the Cross, repeating what the false witnesses claimed in their interpretation of Christ's saying that He would destroy the temple and raise it in three days – while He meant His body – and they were saying: Instead of destroying the temple and raising it, would it not rather be better for You to bring Yourself down – if You are able – from the wood of the Cross?! V. 31: Another group of the priests, scribes and elders of the people took part in the mockery of the Lord of glory, and this mockery was intended to prove that what they had done in killing Him was a sound decision, for if He were the Christ – the Anointed of God – could He not save Himself from what He was in now, and they said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save."

15.19.0.en: As proof of their words in the previous verse, they set a condition that if He were really able to save Himself, they would believe in Him.

15.19.1.en: "Reviled him": that is, the two thieves who were crucified with Him. Matthew and Mark mentioned that the two thieves were reviling Him, while Luke mentioned the same account, and we conclude from his account that both began to revile Christ, yet one of them did not actually take part in this reviling, as St. Luke made clear in (23:39), (see also the explanation of (Mt 27:44)).

15.20.0.en: "Darkness over the whole land": this darkness was a miracle by every measure, for there is no total eclipse of the sun that lasts more than minutes, so how then did it last three hours?! It would have been fitting for the Jews to take notice of this phenomenon, and of this wrath revealed from heaven and nature because of their deed, and to take heed ... but so it is with one who is dominated by injustice and spiritual blindness, who cannot see the simplest and clearest things.

15.20.1.en: O my soul, understand ... all of nature clothed itself in black, mourning for its Creator who bore all our iniquities ... and you, what are you doing now? Examine your conscience and return ...

15.21.0.en: The darkness continued from the sixth hour by Jewish reckoning (corresponding to twelve noon) until the ninth hour (corresponding to three in the afternoon). And at the ninth hour the Lord Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" which means in the Syriac language: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christ uttered it, and it is the first words of the psalm (22:1) in which David prophesied about all the sufferings of Christ, the casting of lots for His garments, and the mockery and ridicule of Him ... as though Christ were saying to the Jews in a final call: return to your prophecies that you may know that everything was fulfilled completely as it is written ... As for those present, some of them thought that He was calling Elijah the prophet.

15.21.1.en: Note: it is noted that the Lord Christ, while on the wood of the Cross, had seven sayings, but St. Mark mentioned only this fourth saying (see the commentary on Mt 27:50).

15.22.0.en: "Vinegar": the vinegar here is sour wine, which has the effect of wine but is sharp in taste, and it was very cheap and was given to the soldiers.

15.22.1.en: So one of the soldiers took a sponge filled with wine and offered it to Him to give Him to drink, perhaps with a kind of pity, but not without mockery, for he said: "Let us see whether Elias will come to take him down."

15.23.0.en: "Cried": this was the last cry that Christ uttered on the wood of the Cross, and Matthew and Mark did not mention whether this cry contained words ... but St. John mentions (in 19:30) that Christ said: "It is finished" as His last words ... and perhaps Christ said "It is finished" with a cry, because He wanted to declare with power that the redemption had been accomplished and included all who accept it in the whole world, and then He gave up His human spirit.

15.24.0.en: At the same moment the veil of the temple was rent, which is a curtain of cloth that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies in the temple, and signifies the separation between the holy God and sinful men ... and the rending of the veil has more than one meaning, as follows:

15.24.1.en: (1) That Christ offered Himself a perfect sacrifice, with which He entered to His Father (the Holy of Holies), by which He abolished the animal sacrifices and the Jewish worship, and it was the beginning of the New Covenant (Heb 9:11, 12).

15.24.2.en: (2) The abolition of the enmity between the holy God, whom the sinful man cannot behold except through repentance, and the acceptance of the redemption by the blood of Christ, who gave Himself for this reconciliation.

15.25.0.en: Among those standing there was a centurion (a Roman), who was charged with supervising and carrying out the sentence. And when the man saw all these events, the darkness, the sayings on the wood of the Cross, and the blood and water coming out of the side of the Lord of glory, he found nothing to say except to declare that Christ is the Son of the great God (God). Consider with me, my brother, the testimony of this pagan man, for he is not of the seed of Abraham, nor was he awaiting the Christ, nor did he know the prophecies of the Jews ... and yet he spoke and bore witness, and his testimony was true ... while the Jews – the called ones – remained in refusal, in stubbornness and hardness of heart and blindness of spiritual insight ... truly, it is the testimony of a pagan by which he condemned every one of the Jews who did not believe in Christ.

15.26.0.en: Many women followed Christ throughout His life and preaching on earth and ministered to Him in a way whose details we do not know, although St. Luke indicates that: "many others, which ministered unto him of their substance" (8:3), while St. Mark mentions that some of these women followed Christ as far as the Cross, though they stood a little distance away, unlike the holy Virgin Mary, who stood right beneath the Cross (Jn 19:26, 27).

15.26.1.en: "Mary Magdalene": she is the one who followed Christ after He cast seven devils out of her, and she was originally from the village of Magdala near the city of Tiberias.

15.26.2.en: "Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses": she is the wife of Alphaeus, who is also called Cleopas, and she is the sister of the Virgin Mary (Jn 19:25).

15.26.3.en: "Salome": she is the wife of Zebedee and the mother of James and John.

15.26.4.en: Thus appeared the courage of the women who loved Christ, for fear could not prevent them from following Him as far as the Cross, while the men disappeared (except John – by divine arrangement – so that Christ might leave His Virgin mother in his care)!!!

15.26.5.en: So it is, beloved ... if the Lord Christ reigns by love over the heart, a person fears nothing, but follows his Christ to the end amid sufferings and hardships.

15.27.0.en: "Evening": that is, before the Sabbath, which begins with the sunset of Friday.

15.27.1.en: "The preparation": that is, the preparation for eating the Passover on Friday evening, and also the preparation for the Sabbath, the first of the days of unleavened bread.

15.27.2.en: "An honourable counsellor": two titles that St. Mark gave to Joseph of Arimathaea. The title counsellor is given to the members of the highest Jewish council (the Sanhedrin), and the title honourable means his dignity, his social standing and the nobility of his character before men. He was a disciple of Christ, "but secretly for fear of the Jews" (Jn 19:38), as Nicodemus also was.

15.27.3.en: Joseph took courage and did not fear the Jews, but put all his hope in the Kingdom of God. For this reason he went to Pilate to ask permission to bury the body of Jesus. And had the Romans buried the body of the Lord Jesus, it would not have been certain to the Jews that He had died, and consequently they would dispute His resurrection.

15.28.0.en: Pilate marvelled at the quick death of Christ, since in the punishment of crucifixion the crucified could remain hanging for more than a day without dying. For this reason he called the centurion who had been charged with the execution and asked him whether He had been dead for some time. And when he was assured by the centurion of the complete death of Christ, he gave the body to Joseph.

15.29.0.en: Joseph bought an expensive shroud of white linen, which symbolizes purity, and wrapped Him with spices and wound Him in linen – and the disciples did not wrap the body – and this was a divine arrangement so that they would not be accused of stealing Him. And Joseph laid the body in a new tomb that he had bought for himself, because the Lord had no tomb of His own, for one who overcomes death does not acquire a tomb, and the Lord was buried in it alone, and after that Joseph and those with him rolled a great stone and closed the door of the hewn tomb with it. And the religious leaders watched the tomb, and they set on it "the guards and sealed the stone" (Mt 27:66).

15.29.1.en: Beloved brother ... Joseph of Arimathaea reminds us here of an important spiritual meaning, which is that whoever receives grace must close upon it to keep it, just as we place a cloth over our mouth when receiving the most holy Body of Christ.

15.30.0.en: It was not within the ability of the Marys and the women to stand before Pilate, or the Sanhedrin, or the throngs of the people, but they did the utmost within their ability, so love took them as far as the tomb and the burial, as though their eyes refused to part from the sight of the body of the Beloved until the last moment in which the eye could see it ...

15.30.1.en: Truly ... blessed and happy is the soul that clings to Christ until the last moment, for to it He says: "He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son" (Rev 21:7).

15.30.2.en: Grant us, O Lord, never to close our eyes each night except that Your image is the last thing we have beheld with our hearts ... Amen. From the Resurrection to the Ascension
